What AI Didn’t Make Cheap

How the job of the PM has changed, and how the products have too.

Jaclyn Konzelmann

Product Director, Labs

2017

A niche problem, in a weird corner of the company

Google Assistant. The speech team. Non-deterministic models.

Now it’s the whole company.

The conversation happening right now

If an agent can write the spec, build the prototype, run the analysis and draft the launch plan - what is the role actually for?

Generative AI made writing cheap.
It made prototyping cheap.
It made code cheap.
What it didn’t make cheap
is good judgment.

Judgment. Taste.
Knowing which ideas are worth anything in the first place.

This talk

Two parts

  1. How the job of the PM has changedWhat I actually make now, instead of what I used to make.
  2. How the products have changedAnd some of the trends I’m seeing.
01

How the job has changed

A lot of this job is about knowing what to build.

And that isn’t trivial.

Years ago

The PRD I was proud of

Multilingual Assistant. Every language pair. Every state conflict. What happens when the setting is half-applied. What the error looks like in each case.

It was good work. It was rigorous.
A career highlight.

And I wouldn’t start there at all today.

When both of those costs drop at the same time, the exhaustive spec stops being disciplined.
It starts being overhead.

What I make instead

Three things

01A strategy docOne page. Maybe two.
02A deckFor the room, not the inbox.
03A prototypeThe thing itself.
One

A strategy doc.
One page, maybe two.

The work isn’t the writing. The work is the cutting.

Producing content isn’t the expensive part any more.
Requiring a human to consume it is.

Two

A deck.

The doc is great for offline reading. The deck is for when you’re standing in front of people and you want them excited right now.

The pitch

Three things, twenty seconds

01A behavior change you predictSomething a lot of people will be doing in the future.
02The space it createsWhat becomes possible that isn’t now?
03The product or featureConcrete enough to picture.

“I can imagine wanting that.”

The feeling they should walk out with

Three

The prototype.

Nobody argues with a feeling. It shows behavior, not intention - and interaction is what brings things to life.

The prototype is the new currency of conviction -
and it doesn’t care about your job title.

Proof

Photoshoot went viral.

It started as a prototype, not a spec. And prototypes now get made by everyone - PMs, UX, even the eng team.

Once it’s bought in

The PRD comes back. Just not first.

  1. Who it’s forWhat they expect, what they need, what they’re trying to get done.
  2. What it should actually doThe interactions. Not a never-ending list of edge cases.
  3. What good looks likeThe gold standard, and how you reverse-engineer your way to it.
  4. The frame the agent operates inThe rules and the boundaries, including what it must not do.
A couple of months ago

The overbuilding trap

Your elegant little MVP quietly becomes the bloated thing it replaced. One perfectly reasonable feature at a time - or one time you didn’t say no when an agent suggested adding something.

A side project of mine. Eight weeks after I published that piece.

Count the toggles.

Nobody sets out to build a bloated product.
You get there one perfectly reasonable feature at a time.

If you were starting today, knowing everything you know now - would you build what you have?

The one test I run now

More is not better.
It’s just more.

But first

Before I have conviction in what to build,
I spend a long time just sitting with my thoughts.

The part that gets skipped over: the time it actually takes to come up with a good idea.

Where ideas actually come from

Curiosity, in public, for weeks

  • Talking out loud in the microkitchenNot because I’ve got something. Because saying it is how I find out.
  • Hallway collisionsSomeone snags on one piece, and that piece turns out to be the real one.
  • Reading, X, talks like this oneSomething lodges. Then it sits.

The building got fast.
The curiosity is still slow.
What you choose to build is most of your value.

ThenNow
Curiosityweeks of itand more of it than before
Buildingmonths of itcollapsed
How this talk got made

Recorded the brief. Recorded myself. Handed both to Gemini. Then argued with it.

You’re looking at the output of the process I’m describing.

Make AI your default first move.

Overcorrect on purpose. Push it past comfortable, find where it breaks, then dial back.

When something feels daunting, ask why.

Most of the time that dread is a memory. It’s cached from when the task genuinely was miserable.

Do side projects. I mean it.

Your day job shows you a sliver of what’s happening. Side projects are how you see the rest of the board.

How the products have changed

Three forces, all moving at once

I don’t have a tidy answer for what to build next. What I can offer is what’s helping me think it through.

Framework 03

You don’t have one user. You have two.

The human user, and the agent user. The system has to work for both.

Framework 03

You don’t have one user. You have two.

The human user, and the agent user. The system has to work for both.

Question one

Is natural language a better interface than your UI?

Not all of it. But there are features buried three clicks deep in a menu that nobody ever finds, where just saying what you want would be better.

Question two

Do I build the agent?
Or do I power the agent?

Both, usually

How this is playing out

  • Salesforce, HubSpotHeadless APIs and MCP servers shipping alongside the core product.
  • FigmaNative agent for power users. MCP access for everyone else.
  • HarveyThe counter-case - legal work is specialised enough to own the whole agent.

Powering someone else’s agent grows your market.

It reaches the people who were never going to sit down and learn your tool.

Question three

One experience. Different people, different paths.

Some hand the whole thing to an agent. Some want to drive. Most want something in between, and it changes with the stakes.

Framework 04

Collapsing workflows

Products used to own one point in a workflow, and went deep there in service of being more capable.

Two questions

Both ends are in reach now

Before

What was the user doing right before they came to you?

After

And what do they do right after they leave?

Making this talk used to be three tools and three sittings.
Nobody shipped me that feature.

A workflow that collapsed

Framework 05

The pitch is cheap. The experience isn’t.

Anybody can describe an agent in a sentence. The product is everything that sentence leaves out.

In the wild

Instinct

  1. How it hands results backThe thing you asked for, in the thread you asked in.
  2. How it nudges you firstProactive, and somehow not annoying.
  3. When it asks, and when it just goesOnly the questions worth your attention.
  4. What it remembersEarlier conversations, and which ones matter now.

You can’t hand a one-line brief to an engineer and expect magic back.
Going deep on the experience is where taste shows.

03

So where does that leave us?

Automating the building doesn’t delete the job. It moves it.

The constraint used to be building. Now it’s knowing what to build, and knowing when it’s good.

An agent will happily build you something plausible.
Knowing the difference between plausible and good is the part you can’t hand off.

Generative AI made writing cheap.
It made prototyping cheap.
It made code cheap.
What it didn’t make cheap
is good judgment.

Thank you.
